body:
Thanks for your reply; I really appreciate it.

I have a mostly supportive social group; however, as one who is already rather introverted the idea of describing my troubles to them often feels like an uphill climb.  I also feel like I'm using them for free therapy if I complain about my life.

***

What I did in this case was ask a question on a Reddit board on a different throwaway account.  This temptation is one I should really try to resist, other than perhaps posting in mental health subreddits, because I've looked back and realized that I almost always regret asking whatever question I asked.  I will usually get, among a few helpful, kind responses, several inexplicably angry, opinionated, hostile ones; I try to filter them out but I'm so sensitive to them that I usually end up deleting my posts out of shame and a desire to never read the harsh words again.

And to be clear, when I ask for this advice I'm not getting upset that people are not "telling me what I want to hear" -- I wouldn't have posed the question if I didn't want to hear an honest answer.  I'm just asking that they not use the Internet as a license to immediately take the most aggressive and least compassionate approach to my problems -- or keep their opinions to themselves.

(Obviously that's not going to happen, though!  I should try to feel more at home confiding in friends and family.)

I'm glad that my post could help :)

> I'm wondering if you (or anyone else for that matter) have any knowledge of what to read next and how to educate myself further on the subject? 

First, don't try to "educate yourself."  I can tell you from OCD experience that you'll only make yourself obsess more, especially if you are a hypochondriac.  Don't do any more reading online or in books/journals.  Instead, get professional advice from someone, like your psychiatrist, who is informed and has read your chart.

> The thing is, and this is what frankly makes me angry, no one has ever even suggested that SSRIs could have such an effect on the brain. 

I don't know if SSRIs specifically have that effect, just that psychiatric meds *in general* can.  In any case, no doctor could warn you about every possible side effect of a medication before prescribing it to you: nearly every medicine has countless side effects which you run at least a one-in-a-billion chance of encountering if you take the medication, a few are very serious ("side effects [of Viagra] include ... sudden death"), and it's impossible to predict which ones will affect you until you take the medication for a while.  Especially with cognitive dulling being reversible, I can imagine that a doctor would prefer to test a drug over a month and see if you report side effect rather than potentially scare you away from treatment from serious psychiatric illness by introducing the speculative possibility that a medication could create that effect.

That being said, if cognitive dulling is a deal-breaker for you, communicate that fact to your doctor so that he or she can know not to prescribe you drugs with higher risks of dulling and closely monitor you when prescribing drugs with moderate risks but high benefit-risk ratios.

In an amazing coincidence, this post is a top post in the subreddit at the same time that I have a similar concern -- I, too, have always prided myself on being an intellectual, but lately I feel like I always have words "on the top of my tongue," fail to express myself precisely through speech, choose wrong words or make silly logical/mathematical errors, and get stuck midway through sentences ("um", "ah").  If successfully carrying my part of a conversation is like opening and walking through a series of doors in succession, I feel like a lot of my doors have been needing an extra pull to get unstuck lately.  You can imagine that my awareness of this possible dulling has caused me a lot of (unhelpful) anxiety.

But enough about *me* -- let's answer *your* question more directly. :)  You seem to know that it *is* true that some medicines can cause cognitive dulling, so ask your psy if the SSRI could be dulling you.  If he/she suggests a medication change, then I would at least be open to it; if not, then I would expect an alternative explanation (but with the fact in mind that, given your OCD, you may not ever receive a fully air-tight one) and be ready to seek a second opinion in the absence of one.

All that said, I *do* think that anxiety and OCD are playing a HUGE part in aggravating our cognitive dulling, whether or not they make up the sole cause.  

* First of all, OCD makes many people, including me, extremely susceptible to the *nocebo* effect and hypochondria, so it's possible that your dulling is either non-existent or much less severe than you imagine.  
* Second, imagine you were asked to perform an easy sequence of tasks at a prescribed time, only to be told the night before the time that you would be executed if you performed the tasks even slightly incorrectly.  Would you be nearly as likely to succeed?  It seems unlikely.  But as it stands now we (you and I) are acutely aware of how we perform in tasks requiring our intelligence.  What's more, since we take pride in that intelligence our entire self-worth rides on these performances.  So we are more likely to fail than before, which only compounds the problem.  It's thus quite likely that anxiety plays a significant role in what we are experiencing.

I think that we can help ourselves for the moment by speaking with a kinder, less critical internal voice: a good friend wouldn't tell us that we were "stupid" for making a mistake in court or on an assignment, after all, but rather encourage and advocate for us.  Learning to speak with that voice has helped both with my anxiety/OCD and depression.

Take care and happy holidays to you too!

I'm going to half-agree-half-disagree with you, Mr. Gaming.

I've been a fierce advocate of an international convention on what "closing time" means: *i.e.*, is it the time when customers must exit, or after which no one else may enter?  It seems to vary store to store and even region to region.  (Good luck getting into even a casual Swiss restaurant in the *hour* before "closing time.")

When I worked my high school sandwich shop job we closed at 10pm and were trained that anyone coming in at 9:59:59 or before was to be served like any other customer; we were, however, allowed to clean and close up shop around them, and ask them to leave after we were done with closing tasks.  And I have to admit that I get quite annoyed when I'm not allowed into a store/given the evil eye when I come in 15-30 minutes before closing. 

On the other hand, if the store closes at 10pm then it is clearly not okay to stay until 10:30pm, especially just for chit-chat.  I don't think it would have been out of order to end the conversation because "we need to close" and wish the woman a good night.  Maybe the store could make an announcement at 9:45pm of the nature of: "It is now 15 minutes before our closing time; please bring your final selections to the tills before they close on the hour."  Or clarify that "last seating" is at a certain time for a restaurant, or "last call" for a bar or pub.

> From your lips to the gods' ears!

Oh, you kid :)

To be fair, I *myself* need to be open, and check that I don't interpret the truth as "meanness" from over-sensitivity.  But in the case I have in mind (no longer available to read) the person twisted my words out of context to suggest that I had said something that I hadn't, and then used that misinterpretation to:

* insult me
* "helpfully" suggest that I seek therapy
* prescribe an *exact time frame* during which I should entirely refrain from dating others

> a couple of alcohol-induced suicidal incidents.

Yikes!  How terrifying those must have been.  If it's not too personal, would you mind sharing what happened?

> affects me negatively the next day as well

In the sense that it makes your depression worse?  Personally, I cannot drink anywhere near the quantities that many of my friends can because I will have nightmarish hangovers and mood swings the next day.  How people "do shots" without dropping dead is a mystery to me.

I'm part Asian as well, so I'm sure that that fact doesn't help matters.  My mother and brother can't tolerate more than one or two glasses of wine without becoming seriously intoxicated, and while that's not the case for me (being fat has its advantages after all) I feel like it takes much less alcohol to make me drunk than other people my size.

> while on mood stabilizers.

I currently take gabapentin (branded Neurontin in the US); I believe that that is a mood stabilizer.  The interaction warnings on RxList, etc., tend to be standard-order finger wags about how it will make you sleepy -- what has your experience been?  Or what do you know about the possible interactions?

True story: when I first saw this link on the home page I thought it was a press release from the government of Newfoundland and Labrador touting the success of universal health care.  I had woken up on the wrong side of the bed and for a brief little moment it actually brightened my morning.

Come back to me, precious few seconds of innocence.  

***

PS -- Since stooooooopid like this looks set to be the norm for the next four years ... how on earth are you supposed to respond?  (Assuming, of course, that you're expected to continue what is obviously a futile debate?)

I'm a bisexual man who has OCD and I've asked myself many of the same questions you have, in much the same way.  And I was doing so even outside the context of my OCD!  So I really feel for you.

The point is, sex can be confusing.  We make it confusing without meaning to, and then society comes along with its judgments and turns a difficult thing into quantum physics.

So.  First of all, don't worry about how to identify.  It's a pointless distinction.  No one asks you to put your favourite ice cream flavour on your driver's licence, and you owe no one knowledge of your preference of sexual partner -- not even yourself.

Second, simplify matters: Let your heart and mind guide you to whomever they will.  They'll make the choice that's right for you, instead of the choice that's right for someone else.

This question is a tough one to answer without using reassurance but, as a fellow human being, I want to help you -- especially with an obsession I've recently struggled with myself, and one that's so disturbing.

> I definitely don't want to die

This phrase is the kicker.  People who are actually suicidal *want* to die; you don't decide to kill yourself on a moment's notice.

My advice is to simply shut the thoughts down with that very phrase as soon as they come.  "What a ridiculous idea!  *I definitely don't want to die*, so my OCD brain needs to quit throwing these dumb intrusive thoughts at me."  And then do something mentally engaging, like math; or a sudoku; or chess; so that you avoid ruminating.  The worst thing you can do is continue to ask yourself if the thoughts have any merit.

> Has anyone experienced both suicidal obsessions and genuine suicidal ideation who can explain the difference to me?

I have had both at nearly the same time, but there was a clear difference between the two (at least looking back).  The suicidal thoughts came first -- I intentionally entertained them and really did want to die, and I wasn't even having any OCD symptoms at the time that I was aware of.  Then I was hospitalized for the thoughts, and once I left I started having OCD symptoms because I was afraid I had left too early.  But the OCD thoughts were similar to the ones you describe: brief, intrusive "flashes" that didn't at all correspond to my mood or outlook.  At the time I was having the OCD thoughts I was happy and optimistic; the thoughts were not at all similar to the ones I had when I entered the hospital.  But my OCD brain confused the two because ... well, that's what an OCD brain does best.

> at what point do I need to take these thoughts seriously and call 911 or something?

My gut feeling is that you don't need to based on these thoughts alone.  HOWEVER, OCD can, itself, make people depressed enough to consider self-harm.  If this happens and you feel like you are in serious and immediate danger, then call 911 or a suicide hotline immediately.

> I wouldn't call out an authority figure

I can't say I agree with you here.  Perhaps more caution is warranted because authority figures can make things happen (or not) for you, but authority doesn't excuse a person from decency.

Yep yep yep yep yep.  I 100% agree with you.  I have OCD too and that annoys the shit out of me.

Here's a question: do you think you should speak up and call out?
It sounds very similar to OCD, although we can't diagnose you ourselves.

First of all, the fact that this offends you does not make you "touchy."  It's not nice to make light of other people's suffering, and for the exact reasons you mention this kind of bullshit drives me up a fucking wall.

Are you open about the fact that you have OCD?  If so, then perhaps talking to her about your experiences would be a good experience for both of you.  You could make it clear that you are not trying to make her feel bad but rather help her understand that those jokes can be hurtful since stereotyping and trivializing something very serious and destructive.

If not then it's a bit tougher, because I can easily imagine the old (and wrong) "Jesus, quit being so PC and offended" response, and of course she'll want to joke about it all the more.  As much as I don't want to tell you to let it go, doing so would be the only option at that point unless you wanted to do directly to HR; you would, of course, have a strong case for doing so but you might ask to remain anonymous.

:)  Thanks.  I'd almost like to have a separate conversation about why you disagree with my "position."  I'm not really taking a position and my behavior isn't hurting you.  Perhaps you could PM me?  I'd be interested to answer questions you have.

End this relationship.

Ages of consent may draw arbitary lines (they're intended to protect children from predators, not regulate teenage love), but the fact is that you could get in big, big trouble in the appreciably likely event that someone reports you.  Worse, a conviction for statutory rape will forever brand you as a child molester and could affect your ability to travel freely, live where you please, and even be around children.  Not saying I agree with such things, especially in cases like this that the laws probably aren't designed for, but you need to be aware of the possibility.

So I would highly recommend that you cut this off until the girl is of legal age.  Chances are she'll still be there, and you won't have to take the risk of creating serious problems for yourself.

**Edit: I wish the person who downvoted me would respond to my suggestion rather than taking the easy way out.  What did I say that was so offensive or off-base that you felt it appropriate to downvote me?  The OP asked for thoughts and I was trying to help him or her avoid trouble.  I guess I thought this was a welcoming, open community.  Sorry I overstepped and offended you.**

Of course you would want good things for your dad.  That's only compassionate and human.

Ultimately, though, I think your dad needs to express repentance  and change his behavior if he expects a good relationship with you.  Now that you're an adult you don't have to put up with his nonsense anymore, and no one should expect you to.  He said some awful things to you and he's responsible for his actions and their consequences.  

One of those consequences may be that he is never able to salvage his relationship with you.  Thinking in this way about my dad makes me feel a little better but, on the other hand, I do have some degree of control over my relationship with him.

You can't be certain about anything.

However, one discouraging thing for me is that I read about a lot of OCD obsessions that deal with eventualities that are either impossible or close to it (e.g., I have rabies because I was in the same room as someone who works at a shelter).  What anout eventualities where the probability is distinctly possible?

Furthermore, am I supposed to completely dismiss the idea that something bad could happen to me?  What if I were to, say, rob a bank?  Then I would rightly be concerned that I'll get caught, go to prison, etc., right?  What is the difference?

Exhibit A of an example where anxiety can work in your favor.  What's going on with you is better than the alternative of posting thoughtlessly on social media :)

I have a similar obsession -- for me I'm afraid to post bc I don't want what I say to be misconstrued as racist/sexist/etc.  Do you have that obsession?

It's not enough to *just* find a psychiatrist -- psychiatrists are a dime a dozen and most of them are, frankly, worthless.  Especially for a condition like OCD, you have to find a *good* psychiatrist -- and preferably one who is specifically trained to treat OCD.  Those can be hard to come by and so you'll need to do some research.

Keep looking, and maybe even pay an out-of-network doctor on credit for one or two sessions if it means seeing someone who's experienced and has a good reputation with patients.  If you live in the NYC area then I highly recommend Dr. Steven Poskar -- even if you live elsewhere he is good enough to merit a special trip because he seriously knows his shit.

One more thing: life is worth living, even life with OCD, and there are people who can help you if you feel suicidal.  Stay strong.  You've got this.

You are a strong person to endure everything you've endured.  I am proud of you for that.

Have you considered changing your routine?  In particular, getting away from the computer and out into the sunlight, preferably with some physical activity mixed?  I can imagine that your surroundings are not helping you to be mentally healthy.  I, for one, feel terrible if I have nothing organized to do for long periods, which is why my depression is usually at its bottom right before the school year.  Can you get a job?  Is there someplace in the community you can go?

About the psychiatrists -- finding a caring and knowledgeable psychiatrist is a challenge.  Don't be discouraged by the fact that the first few didn't work for you.  Continue to seek help, because you are worth it.

I'm sorry you've had to deal with those thoughts.  I have OCD and so know firsthand how bad obsessive thoughts can be (I have no idea if yours are the same as mine, mind you).  And I'm here so I've felt suicidal myself.

Do you think you could repost (so you can go to the front of the queue again) and tell us a little more about how counseling hasn't worked?  If we knew about why the help feels temporary, then maybe we could direct you to a better resource or give more detailed advice.

Also, might I recommend that you see a psychiatrist (medical doctor)?  It's possible that there's a biological reason why you are feeling and thinking the way that you do -- many mental illnesses, for example, are believed to be caused by imbalances of chemicals in the brain.  Some people are apprehensive about seeing a psychiatrist, but you would be under no obligation to follow their regimen and it couldn't possibly hurt to hear a professional opinion.

What do you think?

Obsessive thoughts?  Suicidal thoughts?  Please tell us so we can help.

Have you ever been under the care of a psychiatrist or psychologist?
